notes.meaning: Aaron had four sons who were appointed as priests before the Lord. King David later organized their descendants into regular groups to share the work of worship. God desires holy service to be carried out with great care and order.

Aaron's two oldest sons died during his lifetime after they offered unauthorized fire before the Lord. Because they left no children of their own, only Eleazar and Ithamar remained to serve as priests. All future priests in Israel descended from these two surviving brothers.

David worked alongside the leading priests, Zadok and Ahimelech, to group the priests for service. Each leader represented one of the two surviving branches of Aaron's family. Together they assigned the families their regular duties so temple worship would run in turn without confusion.

When the priestly families were counted, Eleazar's line had grown much larger than Ithamar's. Because Eleazar had twice as many family heads, David created sixteen divisions from Eleazar and eight from Ithamar. This produced twenty-four groups in all, giving each family a fair share of the work.

The leaders drew lots to decide the order in which each family would serve. Both lines were noble and held high offices, so casting lots showed God's choice and stopped jealousy or arguments. Entrusting the outcome to God brought peace and unity to the priests.

A Levite scribe named Shemaiah wrote down each name as the lots were drawn. The whole drawing took place in public before the king, the chief priests, and tribal leaders so everyone could see it was completely fair. They drew families from Eleazar and Ithamar in turn until the full list was recorded.

The first four lots determined the earliest family rotations for temple duty. Jehoiarib received the very first shift, followed in order by Jedaiah, Harim, and Seorim. Centuries later, the famous Jewish Maccabean family came from the priestly line of Jehoiarib.

The drawing continued with the fifth through eighth groups of priests. The eighth lot went to the family of Abijah. Many generations later, Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, served in this exact division when an angel spoke to him in the temple.

Lots nine through twelve set the service turns for Jeshua, Shecaniah, Eliashib, and Jakim. These family heads took their appointed places in the annual schedule. Families from some of these lines would return from captivity in Babylon to rebuild the temple many years later.

The drawing appointed Huppah, Jeshebeab, Bilgah, and Immer as the thirteenth through sixteenth orders. Each leader stood ready to guide his household when their scheduled turn arrived. Even when little is known about each man today, God valued each family's role in His house.

The seventeenth through twentieth lots fell to Hezir, Happizzez, Pethahiah, and Jehezkel. Each group received its assigned position by divine appointment. This system guaranteed that the holy place was continually cared for week after week.

The final four lots completed the total list of twenty-four priestly orders. Jachin, Gamul, Delaiah, and Maaziah filled the last rotations. Together, these twenty-four groups formed a full cycle of ministry for the worship of Israel.

These twenty-four divisions set the regular rotation for priests coming into the Lord's house to serve. Each division served for one week at a time from Sabbath to Sabbath under the oversight of the high priest. They carried out the worship rules that God had originally handed down through Aaron.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some historical scholars argue that the twenty-four priestly divisions were not arranged by David, but were created after the Babylonian exile and projected back onto early history.

notes.meaning: The record turns from the priests to the other Levites who served as temple assistants. It begins with the descendants of Kohath's son Amram who were not priests. Shubael and his son Jehdeiah represented this faithful family line.

Rehabiah's family line was led by Isshiah, while Shelomoth and his son Jahath led the clan of the Izharites. These men stood as heads over numerous households. Their duty was to support the work of worship and help their brothers in the sanctuary.

These verses list the family heads from the remaining Kohathite branches, Hebron and Uzziel. Jeriah led the sons of Hebron with his brothers, while Micah and Isshiah headed their households under Uzziel. Naming these leaders reminded Israel that every family branch had a place in serving God.

The list turns next to the Levite family of Merari through Mahli, Mushi, and Jaaziah. Jaaziah's descendants are named as family leaders along with their kin. Every part of Levi's tribe was accounted for to ensure the sanctuary had enough workers.

Mahli's son Eleazar had no sons of his own, so his branch did not produce a separate line of leaders. Instead, leadership in that branch continued through Jerahmeel, the son of Kish. God preserves the memory of each family even when their lines join together.

The listing of Merari's descendants finishes with the three sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jerimoth. This concluded the official register of the non-priestly Levite families. Each man on the list represented a family ready to serve the Lord in the holy place.

The Levite assistants cast lots in the exact same way as the priests did before King David and the high priests. Older and younger family heads drew lots together on equal terms, regardless of age or social rank. This paired each Levite division with a priestly division so that all could serve the Lord in harmony.
